questions.prompt: Free response (Undercoverage, Nonresponse, and Response Bias). A gym wants to learn about how often adults exercise among residents. It mails a survey to 500 randomly chosen addresses from a list of homeowners, asking "How many days did you exercise last week?" Only 140 surveys come back.
questions.answer: (a) Response bias; the results are likely to overestimate how often adults exercise; (b) Renters are left out because the list has only homeowners; (c) 28.0%; (d) Use neutral or anonymous questions; sample from a list of all residents; follow up with nonrespondents

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify a source of response bias in the question and explain how it would affect the estimate. (look at the wording and at how people like to answer)
parts.answer: Response bias; the results are likely to overestimate how often adults exercise

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Identify a source of undercoverage and explain why it could bias the results.
parts.answer: Renters are left out because the list has only homeowners

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the response rate and explain why nonresponse could be a problem.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe two changes that would reduce the bias.
parts.answer: Use neutral or anonymous questions; sample from a list of all residents; follow up with nonrespondents

solutionSteps: (a) People like to look healthy, so many will overstate how often they exercise (social desirability). The results would overestimate how often adults exercise.
(a) Scoring, 1 point: Source of response bias and its direction.

(b) Residents who rent are not on the list. If renters differ (for example, they may be younger or have different incomes), their views on how often adults exercise may differ and the results will be biased.
(b) Scoring, 1 point: Renters left out with a plausible link to the responses.
(c) 140/500 = 28.0%. People who return the survey may care more about how often adults exercise than those who do not, so the respondents may not represent the population.
(c) Scoring, 1 point: Rate and the reason nonresponders may differ.
(d) Ask a neutral question (anonymously), use a sampling frame of all residents (renters included), and follow up with people who do not respond.
(d) Scoring, 1 point: Two valid changes.
Total: 4 points.

questions.prompt: Free response (Undercoverage, Nonresponse, and Response Bias). A gym wants to learn about how often adults exercise among residents. It mails a survey to 600 randomly chosen addresses from a list of homeowners, asking "How many days did you exercise last week?" Only 150 surveys come back.
questions.answer: (a) Response bias; the results are likely to overestimate how often adults exercise; (b) Renters are left out because the list has only homeowners; (c) 25.0%; (d) Use neutral or anonymous questions; sample from a list of all residents; follow up with nonrespondents; a larger sample has the same bias

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify a source of response bias in the question and explain how it would affect the estimate.

parts.answer: Renters are left out because the list has only homeowners

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Describe two changes that would reduce the bias. Explain why a larger sample alone would not fix it.
parts.answer: Use neutral or anonymous questions; sample from a list of all residents; follow up with nonrespondents; a larger sample has the same bias

solutionSteps: (a) People like to look healthy, so many will overstate how often they exercise (social desirability). The results would overestimate how often adults exercise.
(a) Scoring, 1 point: Source of response bias and its direction.

(b) Residents who rent are not on the list. If renters differ (for example, they may be younger or have different incomes), their views on how often adults exercise may differ and the results will be biased.
(b) Scoring, 1 point: Renters left out with a plausible link to the responses.
(c) 150/600 = 25.0%. People who return the survey may care more about how often adults exercise than those who do not, so the respondents may not represent the population.
(c) Scoring, 1 point: Rate and the reason nonresponders may differ.

(d) Ask a neutral question (anonymously), use a sampling frame of all residents (renters included), and follow up with people who do not respond. Bias is systematic, so a larger sample would repeat it with less variability.
(d) Scoring, 1 point: Two valid changes and the explanation.
Total: 4 points.

questions.prompt: Free response (Confounding, Placebos, and Blinding). A company tests a herbal sleep aid. It recruits 60 adults with insomnia, randomly assigns half to the new product and half to an identical-looking placebo, and measures the hours of sleep after four weeks.
questions.answer: (a) To control for the placebo effect, so any difference can be attributed to the product; (b) Neither the subjects nor the people measuring the response know who got which treatment; (c) Knowing the treatment could change how subjects report or how staff measure the response; (d) Self-selection: people who choose the product may differ in ways that affect the response (confounding)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Why is a placebo group needed?
parts.answer: To control for the placebo effect, so any difference can be attributed to the product

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe what it would mean for this experiment to be double-blind. (think about the subjects and the people who measure the response)
parts.answer: Neither the subjects nor the people measuring the response know who got which treatment

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why double-blinding matters here.
parts.answer: Knowing the treatment could change how subjects report or how staff measure the response

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose instead the subjects chose whether to take the product. Explain why the results could not show cause and effect.
parts.answer: Self-selection: people who choose the product may differ in ways that affect the response (confounding)

solutionSteps: (a) Subjects may improve simply because they believe they are treated; the placebo group experiences that too, so only the active ingredient differs.
(a) Scoring, 1 point: Placebo effect and comparison.
(b) Subjects do not know their group, and the staff who measure and record the response do not know either.
(b) Scoring, 1 point: Both groups named.
(c) The hours of sleep could be influenced by expectations, so knowledge of the treatment could bias the results.
(c) Scoring, 1 point: Explains how knowledge could bias the response.
(d) Without random assignment, those who choose a herbal sleep aid may differ (for example, in how severe their symptoms are), so differences could be due to that variable.
(d) Scoring, 1 point: Confounding from self-selection.
Total: 4 points.

questions.prompt: Free response (Confounding, Placebos, and Blinding). A company tests a herbal sleep aid. It recruits 80 adults with insomnia, randomly assigns half to the new product and half to an identical-looking placebo, and measures the hours of sleep after four weeks.
questions.answer: (a) To control for the placebo effect, so any difference can be attributed to the product; (b) Neither the subjects nor the people measuring the response know who got which treatment; (c) Knowing the treatment could change how subjects report or how staff measure the response; (d) Self-selection: people who choose the product may differ in ways that affect the response (confounding)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Why is a placebo group needed?
parts.answer: To control for the placebo effect, so any difference can be attributed to the product

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Describe what it would mean for this experiment to be double-blind.
parts.answer: Neither the subjects nor the people measuring the response know who got which treatment

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why double-blinding matters here.
parts.answer: Knowing the treatment could change how subjects report or how staff measure the response

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Suppose instead the subjects chose whether to take the product. Explain why the results could not show cause and effect.
parts.answer: Self-selection: people who choose the product may differ in ways that affect the response (confounding)

solutionSteps: (a) Subjects may improve simply because they believe they are treated; the placebo group experiences that too, so only the active ingredient differs.
(a) Scoring, 1 point: Placebo effect and comparison.
(b) Subjects do not know their group, and the staff who measure and record the response do not know either.
(b) Scoring, 1 point: Both groups named.
(c) The hours of sleep could be influenced by expectations, so knowledge of the treatment could bias the results.
(c) Scoring, 1 point: Explains how knowledge could bias the response.
(d) Without random assignment, those who choose a herbal sleep aid may differ (for example, in how severe their symptoms are), so differences could be due to that variable.
(d) Scoring, 1 point: Confounding from self-selection.
Total: 4 points.

questions.prompt: Free response (Generalizing Results and Distinguishing Association from Causation). A researcher recruits 200 adults who answer an advertisement, then randomly assigns half to a meditation app and half to a podcast app. After six weeks, the meditation group has a significantly better mean stress score.
questions.answer: (a) Random selection: no; random assignment: yes; (b) Yes, because of random assignment; (c) Only adults like those who volunteered; (d) The difference is larger than would be likely from random assignment alone if the treatment had no effect

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

parts.answer: Yes, because of random assignment

parts.label: c

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain what "significantly better" means in this context.
parts.answer: The difference is larger than would be likely from random assignment alone if the treatment had no effect

solutionSteps: (a) The adults were volunteers; the treatments were assigned at random.
(a) Scoring, 1 point: Both correct.
(b) Random assignment creates comparable groups, so a significant difference can be attributed to the treatment.
